turn_text: I'm Susan Page, Washington Bureau Chief of USA Today, and this is Capitol Download. We are at the University of Louisville with Mitch McConnell, the Senate Majority Leader. Thanks so much for being with us.
Glad to be here.

You have a new book out of memoir. It's called The Long Game. And we're sitting appropriately enough in the archives at the McConnell Center here at the University. In the bookcase, we have your Cub Scout manual. We have the I Like, I like button that you wore in the fifth grade. So lots of memories here.
Well, I was sort of a pack rat. I never really knew why I was keeping all the stuff I kept, but it turned out I'm an archivist of light, because I almost threw away nothing ever.

You've been a pretty private figure for a politician. You don't usually cooperate with profiles. In the very first sentence in this book, you say that in profiles, you usually play the villain. But in this memoir, you do talk about your childhood and your parents and your wife and your colleagues. Why did you want to write it?

Well, I think when I became a majority leader, which was not exactly something that happened quickly, it occurred to me that maybe it would be a good time to talk about my life in politics and my life in general. And that's what led to where we are. The long game, the reason I chose the title of the long game is that it was a long period. Not an overnight sensation. I've been working on my career for a long time. I actually started with my first memory in life and worked my way forward and my first memory in life was my last visit to Warm Springs after a two-year struggle that I don't remember myself because I was between ages two and four recovering from the polio that afflicted my left quadricep. And that was the last visit to Warm Springs and the nurses told my mother I was going to be okay. They thought I could walk without a limp and without a brace. And we stopped in a shoe store on the way home and bought a pair of low-top saddle oxford shoes, which was sort of a symbol of that I was going to be a normal little boy. And I've had thanks to her tenacity. I mean, can you imagine keeping a two-year-old and a three-year-old off their feet? They didn't want me to try to walk prematurely because they were afraid it would inhibit the ability to get whatever muscle recovery you could get in the quadriceps through the exercise process. So she literally had to watch me like a hawk. She did it for two years, like a drill sergeant. And that tenacity that she brought to that episode, I always thought was, even though I was awfully young, was an early lesson in how if you just keep working at something and not defeated by the inevitable speed bumps that we all hit in life, that you could probably get where you're headed.
